item.title: SU Presidential Search Committee Names Finalists
item.description:
The Southern University System Presidential Search Committee advanced three candidates to the finalist stage Friday after a full morning of semifinalist interviews inside the Board Meeting Room of the J.S. Clark Administration Building. The decision forces the months long national search into its final phase, with the Board of Supervisors expected to vote on the next president in the coming weeks.

Committee Chair Ann Smith opened the meeting with roll call and adoption of the agenda before members began interviews with six semifinalists: Dr. Brian Bridges, Dr. Jaffus Hardrick, Atty. Roscoe Jones, Dr. Willie Smith, Dr. Larissa Littleton‑Steib, and Atty. John Belton. Candidates were questioned on leadership experience, student success strategies, and plans for strengthening the nation’s only historically Black university system. Smith emphasized the weight of the moment, saying, “We’re looking for someone who can lead this system forward with vision and stability. This is a critical moment for Southern University.”

Throughout the interviews, candidates outlined priorities ranging from enrollment growth to campus infrastructure improvements. Several emphasized expanding academic programs and improving retention across the system’s five campuses. Hardrick highlighted the importance of academic support, stating, “Student success is at the heart of everything we do,” a sentiment that reflected the broader focus of the day’s discussions.

After completing interviews and entering executive deliberations, the committee voted to advance three finalists: Dr. Brian Bridges, Dr. Jaffus Hardrick, and Atty. Roscoe Jones. The finalists will participate in additional public sessions and meetings with campus stakeholders before the Board of Supervisors selects the next president. Smith said the committee remains committed to choosing a leader who can guide the system’s long‑term growth. “This is a historic decision for the Southern University System,” she said. “We’re committed to choosing the leader who will best serve our students, faculty, alumni, and the state of Louisiana.”

The Board is expected to announce the date of the final vote soon.

item.title: Under the Stars: The Coronation of the 96th Miss Southern
item.description:
The crown has officially found its queen. On Wednesday, September 30, the Felton G. Clark Activity Center was transformed into a night of elegance, celebration, and Southern pride for the coronation of Kampbell E. Mack, the 96th Miss Southern University and Agricultural & Mechanical College. With doors opening at 6:30 p.m. and the program beginning at 7 p.m., guests gathered to witness a new chapter in Southern’s royal legacy.

The evening opened with a compelling performance by the Southern University Dance Department, whose graceful execution set the tone for the ceremony. “The dancers did well as always. I enjoyed the performance, it was impeccable. The stargazing aesthetic and the music selection helped push the theme and entertain everyone supporting Kampbell,” said Southern University student Taelah Campbell.

Following the performance, introductions honored the parents, mentors, royal courts, advisors, and educational leaders who supported Mack throughout her journey. Each acknowledgment highlighted the foundation behind her achievement and the legacies that paved the way. What was once a dream has now blossomed into royalty.

Gallery • 2 Photos
Knykolas Ross
Miss Southern, Kampbell Mack, shares a dance with her father during her coronation at FG Clark.

As the ceremony continued, anticipation filled the room as she made her entrance, her presence reflecting the elegance and pride of Southern University and A&M College. 

“My coronation felt so surreal, it felt like a dream come true. Knowing that I am a part of a legacy that is bigger than me and representing something so much greater than myself means so much to me. It is the best ending to my Southern journey that I could ask for,” Mack said.

The legacy of Miss Southern, both past and present, embodies grace, poise, beauty, and intellect. With her hard work culminating in this moment, the 96th Miss Southern University and A&M College were officially crowned by the 95th Miss Southern, Gala J.

Marcus and Mack’s advisor, Gabriel S. King, assisted throughout the ceremony. As she leaves her mark on the University, gracefully draped in white, Mack stepped into her reign, proving that at Southern, the crown isn’t just worn, it is earned.

“The coronation was a beautiful event. The committee and I spent weeks planning, and it was amazing to see our vision and Miss Southern’s vision truly come to life,” King said.

To close the night, the royal court performed a ballroom routine. As the queens received their crowns and photos were taken, the evening under the stars came to an end. “Coronation night was a night to remember. Being surrounded by students, staff, faculty, friends, family, and alumni from beginning to end was amazing. I am officially crowned under the stars,” Mack said.

The coronation of Kampbell E. Mack ended with pride and purpose, welcoming a new chapter, and a queen ready to carry Southern’s legacy forward.

item.title: Gala on the Bluff gives Southern students a seat at the table
item.description:
Blue balloons rose along the entrance of L’Auberge Casino & Hotel Baton Rouge as guests covered in blue sparkles made their way into Southern University’s 24th annual Gala on the Bluff.

The College of Business was raising money for student scholarships. But the gala also placed students in a room with alumni, business leaders and other professionals, giving them opportunities to make connections beyond campus.

“We’re trying to teach them how to be leaders,” said Donald R. Andrews, dean of Southern’s College of Business.

 The college hoped to raise at least $125,000 during the event, Andrews said.

The Gala on the Bluff was created by members of the College of Business Advisory Council in 2002 to raise funds for scholarships  and build awareness of the college. Now in its 24th year, the gala has provided students with more than $1.5 million in scholarship support, according to the Gala on the Bluff website.

The College of Business Advisory Council, chaired by Sharon Hill, also supports the college through fundraising, networking and professional development opportunities for students.

Scholarship recipients must be in good academic standing, maintain at least a 2.7 GPA and submit an essay as part of the application process. A committee reviews the applications before recipients are selected.

But the college’s goals extend beyond financial assistance.

For Southern sophomore Caluntay Jackson, a business management student, the gala was an opportunity to put that idea into practice.

Jackson was invited to attend by his professor, Mr. Jones, after a luncheon. He was encouraged to help invite guests and distribute tickets, giving him a chance to take on a leadership role before the event started. He didn’t know what to expect but to show up in a suit and tie. Jackson says it meant everything to him to be invited to the gala, meet important people, and have good energy. 

Jackson said students should act when opportunities are presented to them, talk with their professors and remain open to being in professional spaces.

“Being seen, just being present is enough,” Jackson said.

The gala also highlighted students who have already benefited from the College of Business’ scholarship support.

Poster boards throughout the event featured testimonials from 10 scholarship recipients about how the financial assistance affected their college experiences. Among the scholarship recipients featured on the boards was business management student Pharoh Hooks, whose testimonial described how the financial support helped him focus on his studies, campus involvement and professional development.

The gala was co-sponsored by Agnes Andrews Allstate Insurance Agency, a longtime partner of the College of Business.

The event also brought alumni back into the room.

Chauna Banks, a Southern graduate  of 91,’ has attended every Gala on the Bluff  since the event started more than 20 years ago. She remembers when the event was held on Southern’s campus in the Cotillion Ballroom before moving to other venues and eventually to L’Auberge.

Banks said she continued attending because the gala was one of the few major events taking place on the Bluff. Six of her aunts and uncles were first-generation college students and regular supporters of the gala, purchasing tables for the event, she said.

For Banks, the gala represents the kind of experience that can shape what predominantly Black students see as possible for themselves.

“I believe that you start to change the trajectory of your entire family for generations,” Banks said.

The College of Business continues to build opportunities that extend beyond the classroom. 

As the evening continued, the New Orleans band Royal Essence performed, “ where them fans at”, bringing guests to their feet and filling the room with celebration.

The sound of the drums and guitar carried through the ballroom as guests clapped along, their drink glasses vibrating against the tables with each burst of applause.

For sophomore Caluntay Jackson, that future starts with the connections he is making now.

“Maybe one day, somebody will remember you, give you that job that you wanted,” Jackson said. “Or remember you and they’ll remember your kids too.”

item.title: Southern University Hosts Ecumenical Worship Service Focused on Faith Through Trials
item.description:
Southern University and A&M College gathered students, faculty and members of the university community for a morning of worship, music and reflection during the Ecumenical Worship Service on Monday, Sept. 28, at the F.G. Clark Activity Center.

The service included Bishop Joseph W. Walker III, presiding bishop of the Full Gospel Baptist Church Fellowship, as the guest speaker and gospel singer Chrystal Rucker as the guest singer. The event focused on faith, perseverance and keeping focus on God during difficult seasons.

Walker used the story of Peter walking on water to encourage attendees to remain focused on God during their personal journeys. He described believers as “water walkers,” referencing the moment in Matthew 14 when Peter stepped out of the boat and walked toward Jesus on the water.

Walker explained that when people begin a journey with God, challenges and trials may not appear immediately. Instead, they often experience the excitement and positive feelings that come with starting something new. However, when difficulties eventually arise, it can become easy to lose focus.

The story of Peter served as an example of what can happen when a person takes their eyes off God. Peter was able to walk on water while his attention remained fixed on Jesus, but he began to sink when he became distracted by the wind and waves around him.

Although a university faculty or staff member was not available for an interview about the event, the service still drew participation from students. The atmosphere was filled with worship, music and expressions of faith, with attendees describing a strong spiritual presence throughout the room.

For students in the university’s gospel choir, the service provided an opportunity to participate in worship through music.

Sophomore Ariell Coates, a member of the gospel choir, said being involved in the service gave her a different perspective. “Being in the gospel choir made me have a perspective on the service. I was the one to entertain, and it was super fun,” Coates said.

Senior Jaylia Reed said she expected a strong turnout but was still surprised by the response from attendees. “I expected it to be a turnout, but it was still better than what I expected,” Reed said. “The speaker had everyone’s attention the whole time, and it was overall a good event.”

The combination of worship, music and Walker’s message created an atmosphere that emphasized the importance of maintaining faith during difficult moments. For attendees, the service served as a reminder that even when trials arise, keeping their eyes on God can help them move forward.

item.title: Safety concerns at Southern University
item.description:
Spending time across Southern University’s campus during the day, you feel the rich history and great energy that make the Bluff special. But once the sun goes down, that feeling shifts into a familiar sense of unease. 

Returning home from a late-night study session in the library or walking back from your dorm can often feel like a game of avoiding the darkness. There are areas across campus that are terrifyingly pitch black with dying or non-existent lights posted along walking paths meant for students to walk alone. If you find yourself constantly having to squint to see while walking around campus, you can see why safety is such a big issue in students’ minds. The darkest parts of campus are the street where the bandroom is and the streets by dorms. I was driving back to my apartment on campus late one night when suddenly there was someone walking near the road. If my bright headlights weren’t on, I might not have seen them soon enough, and it could have caused an unsafe situation. 

The darkness creates daily hazards that go far beyond a simple lack of visibility. Pedestrians are forced to walk directly in the street because sidewalks fade into pitch-black shadows, dodging cars while barely being able to see where they are stepping. At the same time, people are flying by on electric scooters moving through the dark, completely invisible to drivers and walkers because many of their rides lack proper headlights or reflectors. Nagging worry in the back of your mind about whether your car is even going to be in the parking lot or if it’s going to be stolen by morning, and campus life after dark feels entirely too stressful. 

When looking at how Southern ranks for safety among HBCUs, Southern often lands in the lower tiers on various college safety and crime-reporting databases, frequently penalized for property concerns and lacking resources. According to PlainCampus, using the U.S. Department of Education Clery data, ranked Southern #1,287 out of 2,072 institutions based on its 2024 reported crime rate, with burglary identified as its largest reported criminal offense category. 

A dark campus isn’t just an inconvenience; it’s a hazard that puts students at risk every single night. We shouldn’t have to dodge silent scooters in the middle of the road or cross our fingers every time we look toward the parking lot. It is time for the administration to step up, fix the lights, and make student safety a visible priority.

item.title: Fighting Back: New Personalized mRNA Cancer Vaccines
item.description:
A technology first used in COVID‑19 vaccines is now being explored as a potential new weapon against cancer. Researchers are testing personalized messenger RNA (mRNA) cancer vaccines designed to train a patient’s immune system to recognize and attack cancer cells.

 Recent developments in melanoma have increased interest in whether the same approach could eventually help treat other cancers, including lung and pancreatic cancer. Moderna and Merck have been studying a personalized mRNA treatment called intismeran autogene in combination with Keytruda, an immunotherapy drug. In September 2026, the therapy gained significant attention after being highlighted at the European Society for Medical Oncology Congress, where researchers confirmed that intismeran autogene became the first mRNA‑based cancer vaccine, and the first individualized neoantigen therapy, to successfully complete a Phase 3 clinical trial.

The treatment is created using mutations found within an individual patient’s tumor, allowing researchers to design a vaccine tailored to the unique characteristics of that person’s cancer. This personalized approach trains the immune system to better recognize and attack cancer cells, marking a major step forward in the development of more targeted cancer therapies.

 These advancements have sparked conversations within the healthcare community, including at Southern University’s School of Nursing. SUSON Director of Student Success, Dr. Rosalynn Thyssen, said personalized mRNA treatments could represent an important shift in cancer care. “What stands out to me is the potential to move beyond a one‑size‑fits‑all approach to cancer care,” Thyssen said. “Personalized mRNA technology may offer an opportunity to develop treatments that are specifically designed around the unique characteristics of an individual’s cancer.”

We spoke with a few Southern University nursing students to hear their thoughts on the matter. Trinitee Thyssen, a sophomore nursing student, said developments in cancer research show how quickly healthcare continues to evolve. “As a nursing student, I think it’s exciting to see how quickly medicine is advancing,” Thyssen said. “Cancer affects so many families, so seeing researchers work on more personalized treatments gives me hope for what healthcare could look like in the future.” 

Amelia Martin, a graduating senior nursing student, also recognized the importance of personalized care. “Throughout nursing school, we learn that every patient responds differently to treatment,” Martin said. “The idea of creating cancer treatments based on an individual patient’s tumor shows how healthcare is becoming more personalized.”

Although the results are promising, mRNA cancer vaccines remain experimental as researchers continue studying their effectiveness across different types of cancer. Still, the growing interest from scientists, healthcare leaders, and future nurses highlights how personalized medicine may shape the next chapter of cancer care. As research progresses, these developments offer a sense of optimism, suggesting that more precise, patient‑centered treatments could one day become a reality.

item.title: September Senate Meeting
item.description:
On September 21, the Student Government Association held a senate meeting in the Mocha Room inside Southern University’s Smith‑Brown Union. These meetings generally cover campus issues, concerns, and areas that need stronger prioritization based on the perspectives of both students and faculty here at Southern.

 The discussion opened with Diretor of Housing, Mrs. Tracie Abraham, as she addressed some of the concerns students have been having on campus, including the recent power outages and the aging infrastructure. She explained that these issues contributed to the amount of time it took to restore power. She indicated that the source of the problem has now been identified and reassured students that Southern is working to eliminate this issue.

Parking was another concern brought up. Abraham explained that although there may not be a lot of parking directly in front of the academic buildings, there are plenty of parking spaces around the Mini‑Dome. She mentioned that she had walked around campus and noticed that this area has a significant number of open spaces. Her point was that students may have to park farther away and walk to their buildings, but parking is available.

After Mrs. Abraham’s portion, the senators representing the different colleges gave their reports and monthly updates. During this part of the Senate meeting, each college’s senators typically provide updates about what is happening within their college, important opportunities, and any concerns affecting their students. They also follow up on concerns raised at previous meetings or submitted by students through the QR code on the SGA Senate Instagram.

After the college updates, the swearing‑in ceremony took place. The recently elected freshman class officers were sworn in by Dr. Walton, along with other officers who had not yet been officially sworn in.

In all, many universities have issues whether they are publicly announced or not, so being aware, hearing everyone’s perspective, and then creating an action plan can help improve the environment around you. These SGA meetings are hosted twice a month at 6 p.m. and are meant for the improvement of the campus, student body, and faculty overall.

item.title: SU Search Committee Swiftly Advances Six Presidential Semifinalists
item.description:
The Southern University System Presidential Search Committee convened for a brief meeting on Thursday, September 24, moving swiftly through its agenda in a session that lasted less than six minutes. During the short gathering, members reviewed applicant materials for the ongoing presidential search and confirmed that no votes were taken at this stage. The purpose of the meeting was strictly evaluative, focusing on confirming candidates who should advance based on their professional backgrounds and leadership experience.

Despite the meeting’s brevity, the committee advanced six individuals to the semifinalist round. The selected candidates include Brian K. Bridges, Ph.D., Senior Advisor at Whiteboard Advisors and former Secretary of Higher Education for the State of New Jersey; John K. Belton, J.D., District Attorney for Louisiana’s Third Judicial District Court; Jaffus Hardrick, Ed.D., former President of Florida Memorial University; Roscoe Jones, J.D., former Dean of Drake University Law School; Larissa Littleton‑Steib, Ph.D., Chancellor of Delgado Community College; and Willie E. Smith, Ph.D., Chancellor of Baton Rouge Community College. Each semifinalist brings significant experience in higher education, public service, or executive leadership.

The committee noted that the next step in the search process will be in‑person interviews with the semifinalists. A tentative date of October 7 was proposed for these interviews, though the schedule has not yet been finalized. Additional updates are expected to be shared with campus participants through official Southern University System channels.

item.title: New Hotel opens just near campus
item.description:
Big changes are coming to the area of North Baton Rouge. With great efforts from Metro Councilman of District 2 Anthony Kenney, a new hotel has opened its doors. Located at 7770 Howell Blvd, this Woodspring Suites has been established to provide housing to alumni and visiting families. The hotel features 120 units across four floors and sits less than ten minutes from Southern University’s campus as well as the Baton Rouge Metro Airport, providing comfortable housing while easing the stress of travel.

During the opening ceremony, Councilman Anthony Kenney shared deeper insight into the purpose of the hotels. “In this particular area, we’re right near the Baton Rouge Airport. It serves as the main airport for the capital region. With more football and concerts coming to the area. We want to make sure we meet that demand when more visitors come to the capital region. And so, we want a hotel that sits right near the airport that brings more capacity for tourists to actually stay in the Baton Rouge area. But most importantly, the Southern University area.”

Along with servicing fans, the hotel also offers added benefits for fans of Southern Athletics. “We are part of Southern Athletics. We have more alumni fans come for Southern University football games and sporting events. They’re going to have a partnership with them and let them know anytime there’s any special discounts, attractions, or specials for any fans coming to the area as well.”, Kenney adds.

Students at Southern strongly support the new improvements to the area. Junior nursing major Lia Thomas shared her perspective, saying, “I think it’s good. Especially for homecoming. People don’t have to travel as far and could be right there. Because Southern is, in a way, secluded. Not a lot of people live on this side. I’m used to stuff being close, so anything that makes it more convenient to be closer to school, I like it regardless.

Senior criminal justice major Yesis Adkins added her support as well. “I think a hotel would be good for when parents come to visit, and the student is staying on campus. I would like to see more restaurants and some entertainment places where the students could go.”

There is no shortage of new construction, showing just how committed the leaders and community members of Baton Rouge are to creating a better experience for Southern University students and alumni.

item.title: Fall 2026 Career Fair: Key Student Takeaways
item.description:
Every year, the Southern University and A&M College Career Services Center hosts an engaging Career Fair for students to network, build strong connections, and get their foot in the door for their future careers. It remains a great way to connect students and alumni directly with regional and national employers to secure professional opportunities. The event continues to serve as a central hub for workforce development, experiential learning, and overall student success.

The goals of the Career Fair are to accomplish job and internship placement, talent pipeline development, professional networking, and next day interviews.

Mr. Samuel Ross, the program coordinator and assistant to the director of Career Services, emphasized the benefits of the event for finding internships during school and securing post‑graduation jobs. “ ‘I tell students all the time, this is the point of it all, Ross stated.’ You want to come to college, you want to matriculate well, and you want to get a job, this is literally the point of it all.” So, what Career Services does is help bridge the gap between the undergraduate tenure and a student’s career. You can never begin too early; start coming your freshman year.”

Trey Smith, a sophomore Mechanical Engineering student, shared his experience attending the event. “As always, the Career Fair was a wonderful experience. It was a great opportunity to network with multiple recruiters seeking students at Southern and SULC. As an engineering student, I was very pleased to see the repertoire of engineering companies in attendance.”

The continuous impact of the Career Fair is evident through its notable achievements, including high employer retention and hiring rates, consistent scale, immediate recruitment turnaround, and broad access to diverse fields, internships, and post‑college job opportunities.

Marcus Nesbitt, an Agricultural Business major, also reflected on his experience, noting how the event aligned with his career interests. “My Career Fair went pretty well,” Nesbitt said. “I was able to speak with lots of recruiters who were in the field that I’m interested in.”

Gallery • 3 Photos
Knykolas Ross
Multiple students line up to speak with Procter and Gamble, a major manufacturing company.

One of the recurring employers, Procter & Gamble was on hand again this year looking for their next talent. When asked about how employers guide students through the career fair process, controls automations engineer, Langston Fogg, expressed” don’t feel uncomfortable, don’t feel pressured . . . the career fair is about getting you prepared and giving you real experience.”

All students are encouraged to take advantage of the Career Fair, as it is both highly beneficial and essential for the next stages of life. Being prepared and taking full advantage of the opportunities available can set the foundation for a successful future.

item.title: SUS Board Meeting highlights campus and connectivity
item.description:
The Southern University Board of Supervisors meeting on September 18 opened with a student spotlight by a young man Jacob, described as grounded in faith, family, scholarship, leadership, athletics, and a strong Southern legacy, led the Pledge of Allegiance. 

The board then honored Professor Michael Gerard of the Southern University Law Center with the Above and Beyond Award. Gerard coordinates the alumni bar exam prep program and the free LSAT prep program, both credited with major improvements in student outcomes. Louisiana bar passage rates rose from 43 percent in July 2024 to 62 percent in July 2025, and February passage rates increased from 44 percent to 52 percent over the same period. Students described Gerard as a mentor who “teaches students to assassinate doubt,” and one parent noted their child’s LSAT score jumped from 139 to 162 after taking his course. 

Southern’s esports program was celebrated next for becoming the first HBCU to win a national esports championship. Coach Christopher Turner explained that “esports now touches nearly every degree track and serves 2,500 students per semester.” HBCU esports National champion Kobe Robinson shared, “I’ve played for Southern since high school, and chose the university because of Mr. Turner’s mentorship.”  Students emphasized that the esports lab is both a competitive space and a place to decompress after stressful academic weeks. The board discussed expanding esports into game development, NIL opportunities, and entrepreneurship, and pledged financial support for championship rings. 

Gallery • 2 Photos
Jalizynae Jones
AT&T Louisiana President, David Aubry engages with the board at the monthly board meeting at J.S. Clark Administration Building on Friday, September 18.

Next, Dr. U. Leland Martin reported that the College of Science and Engineering welcomed 852 incoming STEM freshmen and announced the inaugural STEM Game Day for K–12 students statewide. SU Board Vice-Chairman Reggie Abraham praised Martin’s leadership and reaffirmed the college’s goal to elevate Southern’s STEM programs nationally. 

AT&T representatives presented a major connectivity upgrade at A.W. Mumford Stadium. The new Distributed Antenna System increased network capacity from 210 MHz to 3,100 MHz and expanded coverage from two zones to sixteen. A standalone generator that ensures the system remains operational during outages. AT&T emphasized that the project was a multi‑million‑dollar investment provided at no cost to Southern University. 

During the Academic Affairs Committee update, Chancellor John Pierre outlined student‑success initiatives developed with the National Institute for Student Success. Advising staff increased from four to fourteen, early intervention now occurs every four weeks, and more than 3,700 students have used the new online study tool, Thea. Pierre noted that financial instability has become one of the biggest barriers to retention, with many students unable to register due to outstanding balances. He also acknowledged that recent campus power outages have intensified student hardship, especially for those living in dorms or balancing work and family responsibilities. 

Across the meeting, board members emphasized that improving student experience, academically, financially, and structurally, remains Southern University’s central priority.

item.title: The Table That Never Runs Empty
item.description:
The St. Joseph Chapel & Martin Luther King Jr. Student Center is a quiet yet faith‑filled establishment on the campus of Southern University and A&M College. From the outside, some may see it as just a church or a simple building, but it offers much more to those who look closely. The chapel and student center are supported by people who care deeply for Southern students and understand that home‑cooked meals aren’t accessible to everyone. Through this commitment, the center is actively fighting food insecurity and helping reduce hunger among our fellow Jaguars.

Father Clark, head of ministry at the St. Joseph Chapel and Martin Luther King Jr. Student Center, shared insight into the motivation, planning, and goals behind the center’s new food‑support initiative. He said the effort grew from a clear need on campus: many students struggle to make their meal plans last, while others have limited meals or none at all. With that in mind and knowing the comfort a home‑cooked meal can bring, the MLK Catholic Student Center launched a weekly Community Dinner every Thursday from 5 to 7 p.m., open to all students.

Students attending the weekly Community Dinner have the option to dine in or take their meals to go. The effort has quickly grown into a broad community partnership, with fraternities, sororities, churches, and other organizations volunteering to cook and serve meals. Volunteers are already scheduled through January, reflecting strong support for the initiative.

Attendance continues to rise as more students learn about the weekly dinners. Last week, the center served 45 meals. Organizers say the goal is simple: to provide reliable support for students facing food insecurity and to show that the surrounding community is eager to stand with them throughout their college journey. 

Junior biology major Madison Holmes said the weekly dinners have quickly become a highlight of her routine. “Going to the MLK Center on Thursdays has been a very positive experience. Everyone there is nice and helpful, and the weekly meals are delicious,” she said. Holmes added that the initiative serves both on‑campus and off‑campus students, calling it a unique resource that builds community. “I encourage anyone looking for good food and community to stop by.”

As attendance grows each week, the Community Dinner is steadily becoming a reliable space for students to find both a good meal and genuine support. The MLK Catholic Student Center hopes the tradition continues to strengthen community and remind students that they’re not navigating their college journey alone.

item.title: Think Before you Click: Students Warned About Email Scams
item.description:
Students often receive emails about classes, campus events, financial aid and other important information. Mixed in with those legitimate messages, though, are phishing scams that try to steal personal information, passwords or money.

Phishing emails are fraudulent messages designed to trick people into sharing personal information, passwords or money. They’re often hard to spot because scammers make them look like they come from a university department, a professor, a company or another trusted source. Students should carefully check the sender’s email address, any links, unexpected attachments and any message that creates a sense of urgency.

Mass Communications Professor Dr. Cynthia Stephens urged students to be careful with emails and to verify doubtful messages before acting. “Rule of thumb: When in doubt do not click. Verify first ” Stephens said.

One of the challenges for students is deciding which emails are legitimate and which should be ignored. Sophomore political science major Ariell Cotes said the constant flow of messages can make it hard to know when an email deserves a reply. “It is very frustrating to receive spam emails and not know which ones to respond to,” Cotes said.

Some students choose to avoid emails entirely. Sophomore business administration major Brailland Hamilton said he usually does not open messages he does not recognize. “I just do not open them all; if it is something I need to know, I just have to take the risk,” Hamilton said.

However, ignoring every email can cause students to miss important information. Instead, students can independently visit the university’s website, contact the department directly or verify the sender before clicking a link or sharing personal information.

Students should also pay attention to small changes in email addresses, since scammers often alter them in ways that are easy to miss. A fake address might include an extra letter, a misplaced number or a slight misspelling that looks correct at first glance. These subtle differences can make a message appear legitimate, so taking a moment to read the sender’s address carefully can help students avoid clicking on a dangerous link. Students should also avoid entering passwords or sensitive information through links in emails. Hovering over links to see where they actually lead, checking the full email address and watching for unusual requests can help students spot potential scams.

As phishing attempts continue to target students and other email users, cybersecurity awareness remains an important part of protecting both personal and university information. The safest approach is simple: slow down, verify the message and think before you click.

item.title: Southern Students Attend TMCF Conference
item.description:
It is the job of a university to provide its students with opportunities to find potential mentors and pathways to further their careers. Especially in HBCUs, where many African American students may lack the necessary support. To support its students, the Thurgood Marshall College Fund (TMCF) created multiple programs to uplift HBCU students. Through these efforts, students were selected to attend the 39th Annual Leadership Institute Conference, where they would meet professionals and learn about job opportunities. Out of more than 20,000 potential students, 500 were chosen, and nine of those students attend Southern University.

The conference was a great success, providing students with an abundance of resources and meaningful professional exposure. Reflecting on the experience, junior business marketing major Zion McCann shares, “This opportunity was amazing for my collegiate and professional growth, I was able to network with hundreds of talented HBCU scholars. I was able to tailor my resume strategically to appeal to large companies.”

McCann adds that the connections made were just as impactful as career development. “My biggest moment from the trip was meeting likeminded students who take career development seriously and understand the importance of putting your best foot forward in every place you step foot.”

Along with job opportunities, conferences help students strengthen their skills as professionals and build their overall confidence. This is evident in graduating mechanical engineering major Ja’Korey Kinchen, who shares, “The experience helped me grow both personally and professionally. As a student, it showed me the importance of taking advantage of opportunities outside of the classroom and being willing to put myself in unfamiliar environments.”

He explains that the professional growth he gained was just as impactful. “Professionally, I improved my communication, interviewing, networking, and problem-solving skills. I also became more comfortable having conversations with professionals and explaining my experiences, interests, and career goals. The experience reminded me that professional development is not only about technical knowledge, it is also about how you communicate, build relationships, learn from others, and represent yourself,” adds Kinchen.

The students at Southern University have immaculate staff and faculty to thank for the many opportunities they receive, with one of the leading contributors being the Dean of the Honors College, Dr. Francesca Williams. When asked about the motivations for attending the conference, she shares, “I view engagement with organizations such as the TMCF as an important part of expanding opportunities for our students. TMCF has a longstanding commitment to supporting students at historically Black colleges and universities, and Southern University students benefit from the leadership development, professional networking, and career advancement opportunities the organization provides. This trip allowed students to gain firsthand exposure to those resources while representing Southern University on a national stage.”

Williams then adds, “My primary goal was to learn more about the TMCF Leadership Institute and identify ways to increase participation among Southern students. I also wanted to strengthen relationships with TMCF leaders, corporate partners, and peer institutions to explore additional opportunities for student success. Ultimately, I hoped to bring back insights and connections that will enhance leadership development, career readiness, and professional opportunities for our students.”

Southern University, along with many other HBCUs, continues to raise the bar, providing students with opportunities to explore their career paths while improving upon themselves. These efforts showcase just how important support is to the development of a student.

item.title: Are You Prepared for Hurricane Season?
item.description:
For Louisianians, Hurricane Season is a well-known and dreaded time of year. Along the Gulf Coast, from June 1st through November 30th, those six months are known as Hurricane Season. The peak of the season is from August to October. Natives and residents who have been here long enough know what to stock up on and when. But those who are unfamiliar may not understand what the season entails, or how to be prepared not only to survive, but to remain comfortable.

Kaytlin Matherne, another Mass Communication student, expressed concern about everyone’s preparedness for storms. “Living in Louisiana, hurricane season is something you’re always aware of. People constantly talk about past storms and how to prepare. All you can really do is be as ready as possible, we’ll never be prepared for everything. And with Southern already dealing with power and lighting issues, it’s hard not to wonder how ready they’ll be if a major storm hits. We’re used to hurricanes here, but that doesn’t mean we’re ever completely ready for everything that comes with them.”

Attempts were made to get a comment from a Southern University housing director Tracie Abraham, but she was not available.

Hurricanes happen often enough that Southern University, the Baton Rouge area, and individuals should have plans in place. Recent power outages on campus and in surrounding neighborhoods have raised concerns about that preparedness. Southern University maintains its own power grid, separate from the city of Baton Rouge. After a week of outages, maintenance, and testing, many hope the campus is ready for the rest of the storm‑heavy season.

Mass Communications department media engineer Elliot Dogan offered four main tips for those unfamiliar with the storms Louisiana faces “First, prepare for extended power outages with flashlights, batteries, power banks, battery‑operated fans, a weather radio and several days of shelf‑stable food. Second, be ready for flooding, Baton Rouge streets and neighborhoods can flood even without a direct hurricane strike, so know which roads flood and move vehicles to higher ground early. Third, create an evacuation and communication plan. Fourth, secure your property and stay connected to official alerts through local news and the Red Stick Ready app.”

As students, preparing for severe weather can be difficult in dorms or apartment‑style housing. Additional tips include keeping important documents and valuables in water‑safe bags, such as freezer bags. During a power outage, it’s recommended to eat what’s in the fridge and freezer first, as food will spoil quickly without electricity.

Not being familiar with Louisiana’s climate can be stressful, but preparedness is key. Material supplies help during a storm, but knowledge is what allows you to stay ready at any time. While the peak of hurricane season is now looming over the South, the National Hurricane Center and the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration predict lower‑than‑normal activity for the 2026 season.

item.title: D4vd Attorneys Withdraw
item.description:
Singer David Anthony Burke, professionally known as D4vd, is facing a major change in his legal defense after his high-profile private attorneys withdrew from representing him in his ongoing murder case.

August 31, 2026, during a court hearing, attorneys Blair Berk, Marilyn Bednarski, and Regina Peter were granted permission to withdraw from the case. Burke requested representation from the Los Angeles County Public Defender’s Office and is now represented by Deputy Public Defender Walid Kandeel. The specific reason for their withdrawal was sealed by the judge and is unavailable to the public.

However, the development has raised questions about why a defendant represented by high‑profile private attorneys would transition to a public defender as his case moves closer to trial. Questions have also emerged about Burke’s finances. Testimony from his money handlers during an earlier hearing showed that Burke earned at least $10 million through his music from 2023 to 2025. Despite those earnings, the Los Angeles County Public Defender’s Office conducted a thorough financial evaluation and determined that Burke qualified for its services. The office has not publicly disclosed details about Burke’s finances.

Office of Student Media reached out to the Southern University Law Center to gain different perspectives on why Burke’s private attorneys may have withdrawn from the case. Roderick Jackson, a second‑year law student, said attorneys are governed by professional responsibility rules that determine when they may, or must, withdraw from representing a client. Possible circumstances can include conflicts involving professional obligations, impairment, or serious disagreements over representation. Jackson emphasized that attorneys in an active criminal case cannot simply abandon their client. “Regardless of whatever reason it is, the judge is the one that has to say, yes you can withdraw from this case,” Jackson said. Because the court approved the withdrawal, Jackson said he believes there had to be a legitimate reason for allowing the change. He also noted that bringing in a new attorney could affect the case’s timeline, as the new defense team must become familiar with the evidence and determine its own strategy, potentially pushing the case back.

 Katrell Hickerson, a second‑year law student, said the former attorneys may have viewed the prosecution’s evidence as difficult to overcome. “They know they won’t win the case because of the overwhelming evidence,” Hickerson said.

Southern University Law Center Vice Chancellor of Student Affairs and Professor of Law Donald North offered another possibility, pointing to the financial and reputational pressures surrounding high‑profile criminal cases. “The original commitment may be from a third party, like a sponsor,” North said. “They may have noticed that there is no benefit to stay involved.” North also noted that remaining connected to high‑profile murder cases like this can bring unwanted publicity to the attorneys involved.

Burke has pleaded not guilty. Los Angeles County Superior Court Judge Charlaine Olmedo determined there was sufficient evidence for him to stand trial. His next status conference is scheduled for October as his new defense team prepares to take over the case.

item.title: Tapped In: Walmart announces Tap-to-Pay
item.description:
Great news for shoppers who shop at Walmart! Walmart announced August 21 that it will begin Tap to Pay at select Walmart and Sam’s Club locations beginning Aug 24. Allowing customers to pay with either Apple Pay, Google Pay and Samsung Pay. For years, Walmart did not accept Tap to Pay at its registers. For customers wanting to make mobile payments would have to use Walmart Pay, the company’s payment system available through the Walmart App. This announcement marks major change for Walmart shoppers who have relied on physical cards, cash or Walmart Pay when making purchases.

For Southern University Students who shops at Walmart, the new payment option could make checking out more convenient, especially for those who regularly use Tap to Pay instead of carrying physical cards. Tytianna Smith, a junior agricultural sciences major at Southern University, said she’s excited about the change since she relied on Apple Pay when making purchases. “I was tired of having to use my physical card whenever I went to Walmart because I use Apple Pay for most of my purchases,” said Smith. According to Walmart official website, the decision to introduce Tap to Pay is part of the company’s effort to make checkout more convenient and give shoppers more payment options. “We want customers and members to have choice in how they pay, so they can check out in the way that works best for them,” Walmart stated in its Aug. 21 announcement. Morgan Price, a senior majoring in Mass Communication said she also feels excited about this announcement. “If I had a coin for every time I forgot Walmart didn’t take Apple Pay, I would be millionaire by now because I’m so used to paying with Apple pay everywhere and not bringing a physical card. So, hearing this announcement made my shopping experience at Walmart better.” Price said. The Office of Student media contacted for comment regarding the roll out of the Tap to pay but did not respond before publication. While the initial rollout is happening throughout 2026, Walmart said its fuel stations are expected to receive Tap to Pay technology by mid-2027

item.title: Shaping Tomorrow: Campus Growth In Action
item.description:
Here at Southern University and A&M College, new establishments are being built while older ones are coming down. Recent developments include the Southern University Global Innovation and Welcome Center. These outstanding developments bring new opportunities to the campus community and its visitors. Some may not know why these projects were created or how they were funded, but Huey Lawson, assistant professor and director of Title III Programs, understands the details behind this decision.

Starting off with the Global Innovation and Welcome Center, many people do not realize that it is a multipurpose facility. The establishment is a 16,000‑square‑foot building that can seat more than 700 people in the main auditorium. It also includes integrated administrative offices, EV charging stations, stadium views, and more. The center’s purpose is to simplify guest access, strengthen community and business connections, and support the campus renaissance. According to Professor Huey Lawson, “It can hold up to 750 people in an auditorium‑style format and 450 in a banquet‑style format. Anything from a banquet to a reception, you could rent a floor.” Many do not realize that the Global Innovation and Welcome Center is not only operating at potential but starting a true revolution. An establishment that once did not exist is now helping eliminate challenges that previously limited Southern University.

Ka’Rah Bay, a senior Agriculture Animal Science major, said the Welcome Center and Amphitheater are “beautiful additions to Southern University’s campus,” noting that the Welcome Center offers a strong first impression for visitors while the Amphitheater gives students a place to gather and enjoy campus life.

Adding to that, India Wires, a senior Nursing major, shared that both spaces “make the campus feel more welcoming and student‑centered,” highlighting how the Welcome Center reflects the pride of the university and how the Amphitheater helps students build community.

Now, let us talk about Seymour Gym, located at the front of campus near the first checkpoint. Seymour Gym is more than 70 years old, so it is understandable that the building now shows significant wear and tear. The facility is not ADA compliant, meaning it cannot properly accommodate people with disabilities. Its stairs, bathrooms, and overall layout create major barriers for those who need accessible features. When the building is torn down and rebuilt, it must be ADA compliant, according to Professor Lawson. This is essential, as Southern University never wants anyone with a disability to miss an important event simply because the building is not suitable for them.

Now, we all know that constructing these buildings requires a major financial investment. According to Professor Lawson, each project was fully funded by federal grants, meaning Southern University carries no debt from any of them. If you weren’t sure why facilities like the Global Innovation and Welcome Center, or even the plans for Seymour Gym were introduced, you now have a clearer understanding. These changes are designed to benefit everyone and show Southern University’s commitment to improving the campus and supporting its community.

item.title: New Drivers, Old Rules: Freshman Adjust to Campus Parking Policies
item.description:
Parking at Southern University may become a challenge for freshmen residing on campus, as the university recently reinstated restrictions on student vehicles.

According to Southern University and A&M College’s general parking policy, “Freshmen who live in the residence halls are not allowed to register vehicles; however, those who present valid reasons can apply for a waiver for exception.” Commuters, or freshmen who travel to and from campus, are still permitted to register their vehicles as commuter students.

As per the freshman vehicle restrictions, all residential students who apply for registration must have completed at least 24 college credit hours and have a cumulative GPA of 2.0 or higher to be granted permission. Students requesting an exception must be able to support their circumstances by providing the university with official proof.

The decision to impose the restriction comes as Southern prepares to usher in a large freshman student body amid parking shortages surrounding the residence halls. Eric Reid, director of Parking and Traffic, cited the large number of incoming freshmen as the biggest influence in the decision behind reviving the restriction. “Since we have a big influx of freshman and not enough spaces by the dorms for the cars, we had to go back to the policy,” Reid said.

For students arriving at college expecting to drive, the consequences extend beyond the convenience of parking. The restriction makes appointments, errands and travel off campus challenging.

Nursing freshman Joshiri Chatman of Covington, Louisiana, recognizes the dilemma caused by limited vehicle access, especially when she needs to return home for medical appointments. “It impacts me knowing I have doctors’ appointments I need to go to back at home,” Chatman said.

Other students found that the ban has hindered their ability to meet daily needs. Brihanna Brumfield, a criminal justice freshman also from Covington, voiced concerns about the inconvenience of navigating Baton Rouge’s heat, limited transportation options, and dining hall hours when trying to get basic necessities. “It’s hot outside, not being able to go get groceries and with the dining halls closing at a certain time not having fast access,” Brumfield said.

Southern students are not unfamiliar with the restriction, as freshmen were also subjected to vehicle regulations earlier in the COVID‑19 pandemic to reduce the spread and maintain social distancing protocols. Unlike the current policy, those restrictions were not implemented nationwide but were adopted by individual campuses during the pandemic. In this case, the freshman vehicle restriction is in place as an immediate and necessary action due to the number of students and the parking shortage around campus housing.

The university has procedures for students with unique circumstances that require them to have a vehicle. Students can request an automobile waiver at Parking and Traffic with proper documentation of their situation. This option is important for students with medical appointments or job duties off campus. For freshmen who have recently moved onto campus, the restriction represents a loss of independence while the university works toward a solution to parking scarcity.

item.title: No Smoke: Governor Landry Signs New Marijuana Restrictions Into Law
item.description:
A new Louisiana law increasing penalties for marijuana related violations near college campuses is raising questions among Southern University students about how the policy will affect them.

Gov. Jeff Landry, a Republican, has passed new legislation that increases penalties for violating Louisiana’s Uniform Controlled Dangerous Substances Law when the offense involves marijuana within 2,000 feet of a school or college campus. (Louisiana Act 305 of the 2026 Regular Session (originally House Bill 568, sponsored by Representative Gabe Firment) went into effect on August 1, 2026.) The change comes as Southern University continues to enforce its drug‑free and smoke‑free campus policies, reminding students that marijuana possession or use can result in disciplinary consequences. Under the updated law, violations can result in up to one year in prison or fines reaching $1,000.

The dean of students and Director of Student Conduct, Kelwin M. Williams, said the university’s approach is about more than punishment. “The implementation of this policy is not simply about enforcement. It is about upholding the integrity and excellence that define the Southern University experience,” Williams said. He added that he wants students to understand the policies and make decisions that support their academic futures. Williams said the university’s approach is centered on education, accountability, and student success. 

However, students have different opinions about how the policy could affect them. Amelia Martin, a graduating senior and nursing major, said  “I belive the policy could create difficulty for students who use medical marijuana.” Martin questioned how students who are prescribed marijuana by a doctor would manage their treatment while living on campus under stricter marijuana policies. Martin did affirm that she understands the university has rules it must enforce, but believes there should be exceptions for students with medical circumstances that require marijuana for their health.

Michal Hale, a junior at Southern University, expressed a different perspective. Hale believes the law is necessary because Southern is a smoke‑free campus and that the university appears to be taking the policy more seriously through increased enforcement. “Personally, I don’t smoke, but it’s good that Southern is taking things like this more seriously,” said Hale.. As the law takes effect, students will have to understand both the university’s Student Code of Conduct and Louisiana law. Southern’s administration will continue providing resources while maintaining expectations for student behavior.

item.title: Southern University Unveils New Charging Stations For Electric Vehicles
item.description:
Southern University continues to build up its main campus with the installment of innovative charging stations for electric vehicles. Located in the parking lot of the welcome center, these charging stations provide both students and visitors the ability to charge their cars while they are on campus.

Several directors came to unveil the new charging stations, with the Director of Environment Equality, Ken Dawson sharing the reasoning and purpose of the charging stations. 

“Because of vehicle emissions, there was funding available to the department of environment equality. When that came available Southern had an opportunity to stand up some charging stations” Dawson explained.

“It also takes us in the direction we want to go. Being innovative, ahead of the game and thinking of the future. Because we know eventually there will be more and more affordable electric charging vehicles that will be made available. So we want our students to have the ability to charge those on campus”

Students have much to look forward to for the future of Southern University. With great new infrastructure, the university has shown that it is more than eager to improve all aspects of its campus for its students. Leaving great anticipation for what other endeavors the university plans to take

item.title: Can Students Compete in an AI Driven Job Market
item.description:
AI driven layoffs are increasing across the country and raising concerns for students preparing to enter the workforce. Recent labor data shows that AI related job cuts tripled from February to March 2026, marking one of the fastest jumps since companies began reporting automation linked reductions.

In March, U.S. employers announced 60,620 job cuts, and 25 percent were connected to AI adoption, a sharp rise from about 10 percent in February. Technology companies such as Dell Technologies and Meta Platforms led the reductions, but the trend is spreading into transportation, healthcare, and other sectors that are beginning to rely more heavily on automation.

Businesses report that AI is reshaping daily operations and reducing the need for traditional staffing. Many companies say AI now produces between 25 and 75 percent of their code, lowering the demand for large software development teams. Leaders also say AI tools allow firms to operate with fewer employees overall, cutting operating expenses and shifting budgets toward new technology investments. These changes are affecting roles in customer service, content creation, and other areas that once offered stable entry level opportunities.

On Southern University’s campus, the rapid rise in AI driven cuts has sparked real anxiety among students who are preparing to enter a job market that looks different every semester. Some students say they worry about whether there will be space for them in fields that once felt secure. Junior marketing major Chelsea Funchess said she believes AI should support learning rather than replace it, explaining that “I am not totally against AI, but I think we need to use it for tools, use it for research purposes. I think we need to really try and get a good understanding of it instead of doing everything else.”

Freshman marketing major Ashaki Harris said she is concerned about how quickly AI is taking over tasks in creative and technical fields. She noted that “There are a lot of jobs like architecture jobs where people are not keeping those jobs because AI can draw plans, outlines, and pictures, so they are getting taken out of jobs because of it.” Harris said many students fear that by the time they graduate, the roles they are studying for may no longer exist in the same way.

Attempts to reach Dr. Brian Adams from the College of Business for comments were unsuccessful.

As AI continues to expand across industries, students and educators alike are looking closely to see how technology will shape future opportunities. For many, the hope is that understanding AI rather than fearing it will help the next generation find its place in a workforce that is still being rewritten.

item.title: Granted Jags’ Wishes: $100M Housing Expansion Approved
item.description:
Southern University’s housing crisis has become a familiar headline for students who have spent years competing for limited space, but last week, that narrative finally shifted after decades of concern about overcrowding and rising enrollment. The Board of Supervisors announced on Tuesday, April 9, 2026, that it had approved preliminary financing for a major on‑campus housing expansion. The project, estimated at $100 million, marks one of the most significant residential investments in the university’s history and signals a renewed commitment to improving students’ experience.

The approved plan outlines the construction of two new residential buildings that together would add approximately 850 beds to Southern’s housing inventory. One building will be designed for first‑ and second‑year students, offering traditional dorm‑style living aimed at supporting academic transition and community building. The second building will feature apartment‑style units intended for upperclassmen and graduate students seeking more independence and privacy. University officials emphasized that the project is still in its early phases, but the financing approval represents a crucial first step toward addressing long‑standing housing shortages.

Gallery • 2 Photos
DIGEST File
The Old US Jones hall before demolition. Since its closure amongst other housing issues, the number of housing slots have been limited.

Students across campus reacted with relief and cautious optimism. Many said the expansion could ease the stress of securing housing each semester and improve the overall quality of campus life. Junior marketing major Chelsea Funchess believes the project could strengthen Southern’s appeal to prospective students. “I think that it’ll really improve recruitment,” she said. “As long as it’s not too crowded to do anything. They need to expand the parking lot too so it can be a balance.” Her comments reflect a broader student concern that housing improvements must be paired with upgrades to surrounding infrastructure, including parking and transportation.

Freshman marketing major Ashaki Harris expressed hope that the university will use its available land wisely. “I just hope they utilize the space they have, because there are so many empty lots,” she said. “And I hope they do it in a way where it’s not affecting other people. Don’t pull a UL (University of Lafayette) … they accept everyone and didn’t have enough room, so students were staying in hotels and motels all year. I just hope everyone has a room.” Harris’s remarks highlight a fear shared by many students, that rapid enrollment growth without proper planning could lead to instability like what other universities have experienced, and exactly what Southern University is now working to prevent.

Chancellor John Pierre emphasized the significance of the project for the university’s future. “This is an important step forward for Southern University and A&M College,” Pierre said. “The demand for student housing on our campus continues to grow, and expanding our residential capacity is critical to enhancing the student experience, supporting enrollment growth, and ensuring that our students have access to safe, modern living environments.”

As Southern University moves forward with planning and development, students and administrators alike will be watching closely to see how the project unfolds. The success of this initiative will play a major role in shaping the future of campus life and ensuring that every Jaguar has a place to call home

item.title: Closing the Gap:
item.description:
An informative workshop aimed at students graduating in any of the healthcare fields was held at the new Welcome Center on Friday, April 10.

Many organizations and entrepreneurs came to set up and engage with the students. Humana, Healthy Horizons in Louisiana was one who came and spoke of their Medicaid plans they offer with benefits such as; pregnancy support, transportation help, and over the counter pharmacy allowance. Another organization that was there was Biogen. This is an organization that helps foster a more informed community-centered approach to care.

Though these organizations were great and informative overall, we turned over to a guest speaker who is an Author, a certified public accountant, and a certified financial education instructor. Her name is Holly D. Reid. She came to discuss financial readiness; this includes minimum student debt, making smart money moves, stats, and great advice moving forward when spending and receiving money.

Reid shows us stats of black wealth are projected to be 0$ by 2053.  Not just healthcare students but many of our students overall aiming to pursue a degree have a bright future ahead of them but are at risk of having to be in debt graduating from school, meaning a lot of their money earned ends up coming out there paycheck every pay period to pay back these student loans, credit cards or whatever you have to owe before you actually start making steady, reasonable income. This is concerning because imagine all the years you put into school to finally be comfortable, then your barley making money and retirement looks even further because of poor money management while you were younger.

What does average student loan debt really cost borrowers? Reid informs us having to consistently be in debt and not keep all the money you’re making can impact you through things like “pushing back your ability to own a home 5 extra years, approximately 500,000 in lost retirement savings, that luxury car you definitely deserve after going to school and working for years or even half of a college savings”.

What can we do about this? The money for school resides in scholarships, grants, work study, seasonal employment, entrepreneurship, income tax refund or being a brand ambassador. Finding a job that can hire you over small breaks like H.E.B or restaurants can be seasonal employment, setting up to sell at your school, things like cool cups, tee shirts or even old vintage pieces people might buy can be a way of entrepreneurship, and for scholarships, it is recommended to connect with people so you can find active scholarships you can apply for even throughout the year. “A lot of student’s problem is in the beginning before they get to college, their doing really good, getting all the scholarships they can and then by sophomore year they just stop trying to apply when there’s money sitting there waiting for you guys” Ms. Reid. Overall, working and putting time aside to make money to start paying these student fees now is critical because you will not have much to worry about as far as getting money deducted from your earnings when you’re graduating.

Another main point is where our money is going. Spend and save wisely, before you purchase something ask yourself, “is this something I need or is this just for appearance?”, “Is this something I can gain from or is this just pushing me further from my goals?” Reid closed her meeting out by giving us the book she wrote to help us have better money management called Teach your child to fish/ five money habits that every child should master.

Dietetic Interns Jakyra Allen, and Arlisha Davis here at Southern says “ We wished more people would have come to hear these important pieces of information because I don’t feel like anyone has ever address this before and I think we can be at risk of being put in a loop of always having to pay back money instead of enjoy it.”  “We also really enjoyed this meeting allowing us to network with people and get opportunities for more insights on my field”.

While students are enrolling in these colleges, planning for our future let’s also focus on closing the gap between owed money and getting to live off your own money.
